title: Asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Construct quantum codes simultaneously having constant rate, linear distance, constant-size checks, and constant soundness under a standard quantum local-testability definition.
status: Good quantum LDPC codes are known; adding constant local-testability soundness remains a stronger unresolved goal.
why: Would connect robust quantum error correction, locally checkable entanglement, and Hamiltonian complexity.
key_works: Aharonov and Eldar (2015), *Quantum Locally Testable Codes*; quantum PCP workshop materials.

title: Polynomial-length constant-query locally decodable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Construct constant-alphabet, constant-query locally decodable codes of polynomial block length that tolerate a constant adversarial error rate, for some fixed query count at least three.
status: Two-query codes require exponential length; constant-query constructions with much larger length and strong lower bounds leave the general polynomial-length possibility unresolved.
why: Would permit recovery of individual data symbols with tiny access cost and modest redundancy.
key_works: Yekhanin (2007), DOI: 10.1145/1250790.1250830; Efremenko (2009), *3-Query Locally Decodable Codes of Subexponential Length*.

title: Subquadratic three-query relaxed locally decodable codes
subfield: Quantum complexity and locally decodable codes
open: Construct constant-alphabet three-query relaxed locally decodable codes of length \(O(k^{2-\varepsilon})\) for some fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), or prove that near-quadratic length is necessary.
status: Gur–Minzer–Weissenberg–Zheng’s December 2025 construction achieves \(\widetilde O(k^2)\). General lower bounds do not settle this exact exponent.
why: Determines how much allowing an explicit “failure” output reduces local-decoding redundancy.
key_works: Gur et al. (2025), *3-Query RLDCs Are Strictly Stronger than 3-Query LDCs*, arXiv:2512.12960; Goldberg, Gur, and Saraogi (2025), arXiv:2511.21659.

title: Efficient uniform-distribution DNF learning from examples alone
open: Learn polynomial-size DNF under the uniform distribution in time polynomial in dimension, DNF size, and inverse error, using random labeled examples but no membership queries.
status: Quasipolynomial Fourier-based learning is known. Jackson’s polynomial-time Harmonic Sieve uses membership queries and therefore does not solve this version.
why: Separates passive data access from active query access for a basic expressive concept class.
key_works: Linial, Mansour, and Nisan (1993), *Constant Depth Circuits, Fourier Transform, and Learnability*; Jackson (1997), *An Efficient Membership-Query Algorithm for Learning DNF with Respect to the Uniform Distribution*.

title: Efficient distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
open: Learn polynomial-size DNF under arbitrary input distributions in polynomial time, allowing an improper hypothesis representation.
status: Open since the early PAC-learning era. Restricted DNF classes, stronger query access, and conditional hardness results do not settle the general formulation.
why: A foundational test of whether a simple symbolic class is efficiently learnable from unrestricted examples.
key_works: Valiant (1984), *A Theory of the Learnable*; Klivans and Servedio (2004), *Learning DNF in Time 2^{Õ(n^{1/3})}*; Jackson’s uniform-query work.

title: Polynomial-time Learning Parity with Noise
open: Recover an unknown binary parity from polynomially many randomly sampled examples corrupted by a fixed noise rate below one half, in polynomial time.
status: Subexponential algorithms are known; general polynomial-time learning remains open and is widely used as a hardness assumption.
why: A minimal noisy learning problem with major cryptographic consequences.
key_works: Blum, Kalai, and Wasserman (2003), *Noise-Tolerant Learning, the Parity Problem, and the Statistical Query Model*.

title: Existence of one-way functions
open: Prove that some polynomial-time computable function is hard to invert on a nonnegligible fraction of its outputs for every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary.
status: Open since the foundations of modern cryptography. Candidate constructions depend on unproved hardness assumptions.
why: Underlies pseudorandomness, commitments, signatures, and much of symmetric cryptography.
key_works: Diffie and Hellman (1976), *New Directions in Cryptography*; Goldreich (2001), *Foundations of Cryptography, Volume 1*; Håstad et al. (1999).

title: Does P ≠ NP imply one-way functions?
open: Derive average-case inversion hardness from the sole assumption P ≠ NP, or establish a precise obstruction to such a derivation.
status: Worst-case hardness does not currently imply the needed average-case hardness. Oracle and black-box barriers constrain possible routes.
why: Would connect the central complexity separation directly to cryptographic possibility.
key_works: Impagliazzo (1995), *A Personal View of Average-Case Complexity*; Goldreich (2001), *Foundations of Cryptography*.

title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
open: Construct public-key encryption from arbitrary one-way functions using unrestricted, potentially non-black-box techniques, or establish a stronger impossibility theorem.
status: Fully black-box constructions face the Impagliazzo–Rudich barrier. That barrier does not rule out every non-black-box construction.
why: Would collapse a major distinction between basic private-key hardness and public-key cryptography.
key_works: Impagliazzo and Rudich (1989), *Limits on the Provable Consequences of One-Way Permutations*; Mahmoody, Maji, and Prabhakaran (2012), *Limits of Random Oracles in Secure Computation*, arXiv:1205.3554.

title: Classical polynomial-time integer factorization
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Factor arbitrary integers in deterministic or randomized classical time polynomial in their bit length.
status: General classical algorithms are subexponential rather than polynomial. Shor’s polynomial-time quantum algorithm does not settle the classical question.
why: Would transform computational number theory and invalidate major cryptographic assumptions.
key_works: Lenstra and Lenstra, eds. (1993), *The Development of the Number Field Sieve*; Shor (1997), *Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer*, arXiv:quant-ph/9508027.

title: Classical polynomial-time prime-field discrete logarithms
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Compute discrete logarithms in arbitrary prime fields in classical time polynomial in \(\log p\).
status: General-purpose subexponential methods are known. Special-field algorithms and quantum algorithms do not resolve arbitrary prime fields classically.
why: Would settle the computational foundation of major finite-field cryptosystems.
key_works: Adleman (1979), *A Subexponential Algorithm for the Discrete Logarithm Problem with Applications to Cryptography*; Gordon (1993), number-field-sieve discrete logarithms.

title: Deterministic polynomial-time finite-field polynomial factorization
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Factor arbitrary univariate polynomials over finite fields deterministically in time polynomial in degree and \(\log q\), without unproved number-theoretic assumptions.
status: Randomized polynomial-time algorithms are classical. General unconditional deterministic polynomial time remains open.
why: Would derandomize a basic operation used throughout algebra and coding.
key_works: Berlekamp (1967), *Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*; Cantor and Zassenhaus (1981), *A New Algorithm for Factoring Polynomials over Finite Fields*.

title: Deterministically construct an n-bit prime in polynomial time
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Given \(n\), output an \(n\)-bit prime deterministically in \(\mathrm{poly}(n)\) time.
status: Primality testing is deterministic polynomial time, and randomized construction is easy. Polynomial-time pseudodeterministic construction is known, but full deterministic construction remains open.
why: Separates recognizing a mathematical object from explicitly finding one.
key_works: Tao, Croot, and Helfgott (2012), *Deterministic Methods to Find Primes*, DOI: 10.1090/S0025-5718-2011-02542-1; Chen et al. (2023), *Polynomial-Time Pseudodeterministic Construction of Primes*, ECCC TR23-076.

title: Single-exponential, polynomial-space exact SVP
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Solve exact Euclidean Shortest Vector Problem in \(2^{O(n)}\) time using only polynomial space.
status: Known single-exponential algorithms generally use exponential space; polynomial-space enumeration has \(n^{O(n)}\)-type time.
why: Memory is a major practical bottleneck in lattice computation.
key_works: Micciancio and Voulgaris (2013), *A Deterministic Single Exponential Time Algorithm for Most Lattice Problems Based on Voronoi Cell Computations*; Micciancio’s SVP open-problem page.

title: Single-exponential, polynomial-space exact CVP
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Solve exact Euclidean Closest Vector Problem in \(2^{O(n)}\) time and polynomial space, including polynomial dependence on input bit length.
status: Single-exponential-time and polynomial-space algorithms are separately known with incompatible resource bounds. Achieving both remains open.
why: Would improve exact decoding and lattice optimization under realistic memory constraints.
key_works: Micciancio and Voulgaris (2013); Blömer and Naewe, *Solving the Closest Vector Problem with Respect to ℓp Norms*, arXiv:1104.3720.

title: Polynomial-time unknot recognition
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Decide whether a knot diagram represents the unknot in time polynomial in the number of crossings.
status: Decidable, and short certificates are known on both sides through major results in low-dimensional topology. Polynomial time remains unresolved.
why: A central test of the algorithmic accessibility of three-dimensional topology.
key_works: Hass, Lagarias, and Pippenger (1999), *The Computational Complexity of Knot and Link Problems*; Lackenby (2021), *The Efficient Certification of Knottedness and Thurston Norm*.

title: Decidability of 4-sphere recognition
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Given a triangulated closed four-manifold, decide whether it is homeomorphic to \(S^4\), or prove that no algorithm exists.
status: Three-sphere recognition is decidable; sphere recognition in sufficiently high dimensions is undecidable. Dimension four remains exceptional and unresolved.
why: Determines a fundamental computability boundary in low-dimensional topology.
key_works: Novikov’s sphere-recognition undecidability work; Poonen, *Undecidable Problems: A Sampler*; recent computational-topology discussions.

title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
subfield: Computational number theory, lattices, and topology
open: Decide whether an arbitrary multivariate polynomial with integer coefficients has a rational solution, or prove undecidability.
status: The integer version was resolved negatively in 1970. The rational version remains open despite substantial work on subrings and definability.
why: Would settle a foundational boundary of algorithmic number theory.
key_works: Poonen (2003), *Hilbert’s Tenth Problem and Mazur’s Conjecture for Large Subrings of Q*; Poonen, *Undecidability in Number Theory*.

title: Certificate-aware finite-size scaling atlas for SAT
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Produce a preregistered, reproducible atlas measuring solver and certificate-checking cost across controlled random and structured SAT families, multiple sizes, solver families, and hardware platforms.
status: Proposed experimental target. SAT competitions provide valuable benchmarks, but competition rankings alone do not establish transferable finite-size scaling laws.
why: Separates solver progress, instance selection, hardware effects, and proof overhead; finite experiments must not be presented as proofs of ETH or P ≠ NP.
key_works: Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser (2025), *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*; Mitchell, Selman, and Levesque (1992), *Hard and Easy Distributions of SAT Problems*.

title: Certified planted-clique computation frontier
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Map recovery probability, wall-clock cost, memory, and energy against \(n\) and planted-clique size using preregistered generators, held-out seeds, and independently checked recovered cliques.
status: Proposed measurement target; theoretical thresholds and restricted-model lower bounds do not provide a hardware-normalized empirical frontier.
why: Tests where asymptotic algorithmic distinctions become observable and prevents cherry-picked “below-threshold” claims.
key_works: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov (1998); Barak et al. (2016), arXiv:1604.03084.

title: Proof-certified MCSP benchmark corpus
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Build a public corpus of truth tables with independently checkable circuit-size upper and lower certificates, explicit unknown cases, and train/test splits that control isomorphism and transformation leakage.
status: Proposed data target. Existing hardness theorems do not supply a standardized, certificate-backed empirical benchmark for circuit minimization.
why: Enables meaningful evaluation of search, synthesis, and learned circuit-minimization methods.
key_works: Hirahara and Ilango (2025), *NP-Hardness of the Minimum Circuit Size Problem from Well-Studied Assumptions*; metacomplexity open-problem collection.

title: Adaptive-adversary dynamic-graph benchmark
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Create a replayable benchmark in which graph updates may depend on previous outputs, with explicit correctness certificates and measurement of worst-case latency, rebuilds, memory, and random-seed exposure.
status: Proposed benchmark target. Theoretical distinctions between oblivious and adaptive adversaries are not captured by ordinary fixed update traces.
why: Tests whether practical dynamic algorithms survive the adversary model claimed in their analysis.
key_works: Henzinger et al. (2015), OMv framework, arXiv:1504.06148; Christiansen (2025), *Algorithms for Dynamic Graphs*.

title: Interoperable formal library of complexity reductions
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Build a versioned library of machine-checked reductions whose certificates record the source and target problems, promise conditions, computational model, encoding, and exact resource overhead.
status: Proposed engineering target, not a claim that formalized reductions do not exist. The challenge is interoperable coverage and auditable composition across theorem provers and models.
why: Would prevent incorrect reuse of reductions and support trustworthy automated complexity research.
key_works: The mathlib Community (2020), *The Lean Mathematical Library*, arXiv:1910.09336; Cook (1971); Karp (1972).

title: Tenfold faster exact maximum flow on a frozen diverse corpus
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Achieve at least a tenfold geometric-mean end-to-end speedup over a declared baseline on a preregistered diverse corpus, including parsing and certificate verification, without losing exactness or exceeding a stated memory budget.
status: Proposed engineering moonshot. Almost-linear asymptotics do not automatically imply such practical gains.
why: Converts theoretical progress into measurable value on real optimization workloads.
key_works: Chen et al. (2022), *Maximum Flow and Minimum-Cost Flow in Almost-Linear Time*, arXiv:2203.00671; Goldberg and Tarjan’s push–relabel work.

title: Tenfold faster end-to-end trusted SAT proof checking
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Reduce total time for proof generation, conversion, transport, and independently trusted checking by at least tenfold on a fixed benchmark suite, with no reduction in the verified logical guarantee.
status: Proposed moonshot. Verified LRAT/LPR, GRAT, and pseudo-Boolean checkers already exist; the unsolved target is the specified end-to-end improvement, not basic proof-checker existence.
why: Makes certified computation less expensive than rerunning untrusted solvers.
key_works: Tan, Heule, and Myreen, *Verified LRAT and LPR Proof Checking with cake_lpr*; SAT Competition 2025 checking requirements.

title: Cross-platform energy-to-verified-solution benchmark
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Establish a reproducible benchmark comparing algorithms by joules per independently verified solution, including preprocessing, failed runs, data movement, and certificate checking.
status: Proposed data and measurement target. Runtime rankings and coarse carbon estimators do not by themselves provide this controlled comparison.
why: Reveals whether asymptotic or hardware speedups actually reduce total energy consumption.
key_works: Lannelongue, Grealey, and Inouye (2021), *Green Algorithms: Quantifying the Carbon Footprint of Computation*, DOI: 10.1002/advs.202100707; SAT Competition 2025 methodology.

title: Sustainable staffing and funding for independent cloud-algorithm evaluation
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Establish a funded, independently operated cloud-evaluation track with public cost accounting, reproducible environments, archived artifacts, and staffing sufficient for repeated annual operation.
status: A concrete operational gap is documented: SAT Competition 2025 skipped its cloud track because it was too demanding for the AWS organizers. Long-term funded operation is the target here, not an assertion about the current 2026 track.
why: Without durable operational capacity, cloud-scale algorithm claims lose an independent comparison venue.
key_works: Codel, Fazekas, Heule, and Iser (2025), *The Results of SAT Competition 2025*, slide 6.

title: Versioned million-problem registry with resolution tracking
subfield: Experimental algorithms, benchmarks, infrastructure, and funding
open: Build a registry capable of maintaining at least one million granular problem records with canonical statements, aliases, model restrictions, provenance, typed dependencies, and auditable resolution histories.
status: Proposed infrastructure target. TOPP, SIGACT’s open-problem columns, and newer open-mathematics initiatives provide useful precedents, but not the specified integrated scale and validation contract.
why: Prevents solved problems from being repeatedly proposed and makes cross-domain research opportunities discoverable.
key_works: Mitchell and O’Rourke, *The Open Problems Project*; Gasarch, SIGACT open-problem archive; Tao (2026), *Open Problems, Open Mathematics*.

title: P versus NP problem
open: The P vs NP problem is a major unsolved question in computer science that asks whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified by a computer (NP) can also be quickly solved by a computer (P). This question has profound implications for fields such as cryptography, algorithm design, and computational theory
